number.why: The arm counts are correctly transcribed for AAD during two weeks of follow-up. Agreement is limited to those counts: the published effect is an unadjusted OR with a 95% CI, not a reported RR. As the ruling acknowledges, following patients 'as per protocol' does not establish either a per-protocol or intention-to-treat analysis.

quotes.span: The primary outcome was the incidence of AAD during 2 weeks of follow-up.

The proportion of patients experiencing AAD during follow-up was 19.3% (106/549) in the probiotic group vs 17.9% (103/577) in the placebo group (unadjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% confidence interval 0.82-1.49, P = 0.53).
Both groups were followed up as per protocol.

entry.why: The methods describe patients aged over 55 but do not explicitly establish antibiotic receipt at entry. The background association between antibiotic consumption and AAD does not establish that eligibility criterion.

quotes.span: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (AAD) is a side-effect of antibiotic consumption and probiotics have been shown to reduce AAD.

A multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial was conducted to evaluate the role of Lactobacillus casei DN114001 (combined as a drink with two regular yoghurt bacterial strains) in reducing AAD and Clostridioides difficile infection in patients aged over 55 years.

missed: The abstract contains an unresolved denominator discrepancy: cache/probiotics-aad-prevention/records.json#/records/156 states "A total of 1127 patients" and "were randomized to the active group (N = 549) or placebo group (N = 577)." Those arm totals sum to 1126. This does not change the printed outcome counts or justify substituting another denominator, but it further limits confirmation of the served intention-to-treat population.
